title.en: Beginning with Shabbos, commanded at Marah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens a series of talks on avodas Hashem and begins with Shabbos, 'the first of the holy days'. He notes that he mostly repeats what is written in the holy sefarim, and that Shabbos was commanded at Marah, before Matan Torah, because it could not wait the forty-nine days.

title.en: Two luchos, two reasons for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Shabbos commandment of the first luchos, 'zachor', whose reason is the six days of creation, and of the second luchos given after the sin, 'shamor', whose reason is the Exodus from Egypt. He notes that Kiddush on Friday night says both.

title.en: The wonders of creation and why heretics deny them

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the beauty of the world through the seasons, the fruits with their different colors and tastes, the human body and even a tiny fly, all showing the Creator. He says heretics refuse to admit it because they would have to obey, and tells of a woman who asked a newspaper to stop writing about the miracles of a war in Eretz Yisroel because they kept her from going to the beach on Shabbos.

title.en: The falling ceiling in Telz

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a club of irreligious young men in Telz where one of them took his own life, after which the plaster of the ceiling below kept falling. Rav Bloch, the Rosh Yeshivah, answered from Shulchan Aruch that blood of the dead must be buried; once the soaked floorboards were buried the ceiling held, and one of the young men stopped coming to the club because he now saw there is a Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: The parable of the painting

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chovos HaLevavos's parable of a beautiful painting that someone claims came about when a wind spilled bottles of paint onto paper, and adds a house that built itself. Nobody would believe that, yet the heretic believes the far more wondrous world made itself, because he does not want to admit the truth he knows.

title.en: The Exodus and Matan Torah, seen by millions

summary.en: The Mashgiach says there was one time when the truth had to be admitted: the Exodus, with the ten plagues that correspond to the ten utterances of creation and the splitting of the sea, seen by millions and handed down as history. At Matan Torah every Jew became a prophet and heard Hashem speak, and no other nation has such a tradition.

title.en: Why the reason changed after the golden calf

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his opening question: as prophets, like the Ba'al HaTanya who saw the Creator when he looked at the ceiling, the Jews at Matan Torah saw the Creator in the world, so the first luchos give creation as the reason for Shabbos. After the golden calf they lost that sight, so the second luchos point to the Exodus they had witnessed, whose ten plagues repeat the ten utterances of creation in reverse order.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that melachah is the product of the curse after Adam's sin while Shabbos is pure blessing, so Shabbos is kept not as a day of rest from labor but as a holy day whose kedushah enters even its simple foods.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by contrasting melachah with blessing. In Gan Eden bread and garments grew ready on the trees; only after the sin did bread and clothing require long chains of labor, and the thirty-nine melachos correspond to the curses given to Adam, Chavah, the earth and the serpent. Shabbos, which Hashem blessed, is therefore free of melachah, and lesser holy days allow correspondingly more work; in the future, when everything is blessing, every day will be Shabbos. The rest of Shabbos must be for Heaven's sake: Moshe won a weekly day off for the slaves in Egypt on practical grounds, but at Sinai Hashem commanded Shabbos as holiness. Through the Beis Aharon's three levels in Yismechu, stories of tzaddikim and their Shabbos food, and the Shabbos lights, the Mashgiach shows that the kedushah of Shabbos enters its simple foods, and closes that oneg Shabbos is joy in that kedushah.

en: Melachah came into the world through the curse after Adam's sin; before it, bread and garments grew ready on the trees of Gan Eden.
Shabbos is a time of blessing, which is why no melachah is done on it; the more blessing a day holds, the less melachah it allows.
Resting on Shabbos must be for Heaven's sake, not in order to recover from the week's work.
The Jews kept a day of rest in Egypt as weary slaves, but the Torah commands Shabbos because it is a holy day through which Hashem sanctifies them.
The kedushah of Shabbos enters its lights and its foods, so that even simple Shabbos dishes have a heavenly taste.
Oneg Shabbos is joy with the kedushah of Shabbos, not merely enjoying more food.

title.en: Melachah as the opposite of blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in Gan Eden Adam needed no work, since bread and garments grew on the trees, and that Adam stayed in Gan Eden over Shabbos after the sin. After the curse, bread and clothing require long chains of melachos, and the thirty-nine melachos correspond to the curses received after the sin.

title.en: Shabbos is blessing, so no melachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that because Hashem blessed Shabbos it has no melachah, while Yom Tov, Chol Hamoed and Rosh Chodesh, with less kedushah, allow progressively more work. In the future everything will grow as blessing and it will be a day that is all Shabbos; meanwhile the rest of Shabbos must be for Heaven's sake, not for recovering from the week.

title.en: Moshe's day of rest in Egypt

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Moshe persuaded Pharaoh to give the exhausted Jews a weekly day off so they would work better, which he compares to the modern law of diminishing returns, and Moshe chose Shabbos. He then explains the pasuk 'Ach es Shabsosai tishmoru': no longer a slave's day off as in Egypt, but Shabbos kept as a holy day.

title.en: Three levels of keeping Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Beis Aharon on the three groups named in Yismechu: shomrei Shabbos who rest, korei oneg who make Shabbos a delight, and mekadshei shevi'i who make it holy, the level Hashem desires. He applies this to rising early to learn, leaving time to learn on Shabbos afternoon, and davening better on Shabbos.

title.en: Stories of the taste of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a poor chassid who asked Hashem to give him Shabbos for his challah, brings the Midrash about the gentile who asked a Tanna what gave his food its taste and was answered 'Shabbos', and tells the story of the cholent of Reb Yechezkel of Kuzmir, whose secret was that he put in a handful himself with the words 'l'kavod Shabbos'.

title.en: Shabbos lights and simple Shabbos foods

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos light and Shabbos food differ from those of the week, bringing the Midrash that Hashem blessed Shabbos with the light, and says the purer a Jew is from sin the more kedushah shines in them. The Shabbos dishes are simple, yet have a heavenly taste, and he tells how a chassid of Reb Aharon of Karlin said Nishmas while preparing the fish, and the Rebbe sensed Nishmas in it.

title.en: A Shabbosdik kugel, not a kugeldik Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Jews eat the same Shabbos foods in a set order because of the secrets in them, and explains the zemer Menuchah v'Simchah's line 'Nishmas kol chai… echol b'simchah' as eating the Nishmas that was said over the fish. He closes with a tzaddik's saying that some have a Shabbosdik kugel and others a kugeldik Shabbos: oneg Shabbos is joy with its kedushah, kept for Heaven's sake.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the self-serving kindness of the nations, whose animal soul comes from the impure klipos, with a Jew's ability to act purely for Hashem, and then opens Tanya chapter two: the Jew's second soul is 'truly a part of G-d above'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah, which can be elevated, while that of the nations comes from the three impure klipos; therefore, as the Gemara says, the kindness of the nations is a sin, done for themselves. He shows the opposite with Yaakov's seven years for Rachel, which seemed like a few days because his love was spiritual, like a tzaddik's longing for a mitzvah. Love for a thing one consumes is really self-love, and even tzedakah or martyrdom can be for oneself; a Jew can lift his compassion and even his eating to be for Hashem. Answering a question, he digresses to the Zohar: Rachel is the aspect of Yovel, of return and redemption, explaining theft, the Hebrew servant, Shabbos, Chanukah, Yaakov's grief at Rachel's death and Migdal Eder. Finally he opens Tanya chapter two: the Jewish soul is G-dliness 'mamash', breathed from Hashem's inwardness.

en: A Jew's animal soul is from klipas nogah and can be elevated; that of the nations is from the three impure klipos and cannot, so their kindness is done for themselves.
Yaakov's seven years seemed like a few days because his love for Rachel was spiritual, like a tzaddik's longing to do a mitzvah.
Most human love is self-love; even giving tzedakah or giving one's life can be for one's own satisfaction or fame.
A Jew's compassion also comes from the animal soul, but he can work on himself to act purely for Hashem, and even his eating can be elevated.
Following the Zohar, Rachel is the aspect of Yovel, return to the root and redemption, which is why Yaakov worked seven years for her.
The Tanya's word 'mamash' is exact: the second soul of a Jew is actual G-dliness, breathed from Hashem's inwardness.

title.en: Klipas nogah and the kindness of the nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew's animal soul is from klipas nogah, which can be raised to good, while that of the nations is from the three impure klipos, as in the Eitz Chaim. He brings the Gemara in Bava Basra that the kindness of the nations is a sin, since they cannot act purely for Hashem.

title.en: Yaakov's seven years for Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why seven years of waiting seemed to Yaakov like a few days, and explains that his love for Rachel was spiritual, like Rav Nachum of Chernobyl longing for the esrog or a person building a sukkah. Yaakov's kiss was like kissing tefillin.

title.en: Loving oneself versus loving Hashem

summary.en: With the man who 'loves chicken', the Mashgiach shows that most love is self-love. He contrasts tzedakah given out of love of Hashem with giving to calm one's own feelings or to win honor, explains 'chesed le'umim chatas' this way, and says a Jew can lift his compassion to be purely for Hashem.

title.en: Exceptions, and elevating a steak

summary.en: Answering a question, the Mashgiach says exceptional individuals among the nations carry sparks of Jewish souls, as with converts. He explains that a Jew's eating, from klipas nogah, can be elevated when done for Hashem or used for learning, while forbidden food cannot be raised until the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Rachel and Yovel: everything returns to its root

summary.en: Bringing the Zohar on Yaakov's seven years, the Mashgiach explains Yovel as return to the root: every person's portion holds sparks only he can elevate. A thief takes another's portion, and a Hebrew servant, who lost the forty days of Torah, falls to a shifchah; Shabbos returns him, and Yovel frees even one who wishes to stay.

title.en: Chanukah as Yovel; Rachel and Moshiach

summary.en: Going off on a tangent before Chanukah, the Mashgiach explains with the Me'or Einayim that wicks and oils not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah: souls Shabbos cannot lift, Chanukah, the eighth like Yovel, can. Rachel, who unites Klal Yisrael, is the shofar of Moshiach and the ingathering, buried near Beis Lechem, and Yaakov worked seven years to reach Yovel through her.

title.en: Rachel's death and Migdal Eder

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Yaakov himself offered the seven years, and brings the Zohar that Rachel's death was his greatest suffering: he felt the geulah taken away. He then brings the Targum Yonasan and the passuk in Michah that Migdal Eder is where Moshiach will be revealed, Hashem's consolation to Yaakov, and takes a question about Leah.

title.en: The second soul: G-dliness 'mamash'

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter two and stresses that every word is exact, so 'mamash' means actually. Unlike the animal soul shared with all creatures, the second soul is G-dliness itself; he brings the Zohar that Hashem, the Torah and Yisrael are one, the passuk 'vayipach b'apav', the bracha Elokai neshamah, and that one who blows, blows from within himself.

title.en: Neshamah and breath; 'alu b'machshavah'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that neshamah also means breath, a person's inwardness, as seen in Rus's kiss of Naomi against Orpah's. He then reads that Yisrael 'arose in thought' first, the reason for creation, and notes the Tanya writes 'by way of a parable' here, since Hashem's thought is unlike ours.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos is a gift Hashem sanctified from above, yet a Jew only feels its holiness when he prepares himself for it all week, like a clean cup for precious wine.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the difference in kiddush: on Yom Tov one says 'who sanctifies Israel and the seasons', on Shabbos only 'who sanctifies the Shabbos'. Shabbos was fixed and sanctified by Hashem at Creation, while Yom Tov depends on the Jews who sanctify the months and on how they prepare, as with removing chametz, which the Radvaz, following the Zohar, identifies with the yetzer hara, counting the Omer before Shavuos, and Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur before Sukkos. Shabbos, by contrast, is a gift from Hashem's treasury. Yet a precious gift needs a clean vessel: expensive wine poured into a dirty cup tastes of nothing. Through stories of tzaddikim and chassidim, the Gemara's account of the Amoraim preparing for Shabbos, and Shammai who ate all week in honor of Shabbos, the Mashgiach teaches that the whole week, with teshuvah and mikvah before Shabbos, is the preparation that lets one feel Shabbos.

en: Shabbos was fixed and sanctified by Hashem, while the holiness of Yom Tov comes through the Jews, who sanctify the months and prepare for each festival.
Each Yom Tov has its own preparation: removing chametz, which stands for the yetzer hara, before Pesach; the Omer before Shavuos; Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur before Sukkos.
Shabbos is a gift from Hashem's treasury, but like precious wine it needs a clean vessel; one who comes to Shabbos unprepared does not taste it.
The preparation for Shabbos is the whole week: learning, davening, guarding the eyes, thoughts and mouth, beginning already on Motzaei Shabbos.
Even the great Amoraim stopped learning to prepare for Shabbos with their own hands, and Shammai ate all week in honor of Shabbos.
Before Shabbos one must do teshuvah and immerse in the mikvah, and the Mashgiach adds that immersing on Shabbos morning is greater still.

title.en: Who sanctifies Shabbos and who Yom Tov

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Yom Tov kiddush says 'who sanctifies Israel and the seasons' while Shabbos says only 'who sanctifies the Shabbos'. He explains that Hashem fixed Shabbos at Creation, while the Jews fix Yom Tov through the months, and each festival is because of them; on a deeper level, holiness either comes down as Hashem's gift or is drawn by the Jews sanctifying themselves.

title.en: Yom Tov's holiness and preparing for Pesach

summary.en: Like a sofer who makes a Sefer Torah holy, the Jews make Yom Tov holy by preparing for it, while Hashem Himself blessed and sanctified Shabbos. The Mashgiach applies this to Pesach: removing chametz, with a story of Rav Yisrael of Vizhnitz and his gabbai at bedikas chametz, and the Radvaz's answer, from the Zohar, that the stringency of chametz is because it is the yetzer hara.

title.en: Shavuos, Sukkos, and Shabbos as a gift

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the preparation of the Omer days, refining one's middos, before Shavuos, and of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur and the four days before Sukkos. Shabbos is different: he brings 'see that Hashem gave you the Shabbos' and the Gemara that Shabbos is a good gift from Hashem's treasury, which one must make known so the Jews value it.

title.en: Fine wine in a dirty cup

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives a mashal of a hundred-dollar bottle of wine poured into a cup left dirty with sour milk, which tastes of nothing because the vessel is soiled. A Jew who did teshuvah, went to the mikvah and sang 'Kah Echsof' before Shabbos receives the gift in a clean cup and feels the holiness of Shabbos.

title.en: Coming to Shabbos unprepared

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes bochurim who spend Erev Shabbos playing ball and then have no taste in Shabbos, and tells of bochurim who came to him with this complaint, one of whom found taste after davening in Stolin. He brings the Zohar that 'Bereishis' spells 'yarei Shabbos', fear of Shabbos, and says one must make a cheshbon hanefesh and prepare all week, from Motzaei Shabbos.

title.en: Every mitzvah toward an uplifted Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from sefarim that every mitzvah and every daf of Gemara should be done with the intent to merit an uplifted Shabbos, and a segulah of tzaddikim to bless one another on Thursday night. Since Shabbos is a gift from a very high place, no one can prepare enough; he tells of a poor Karliner chassid who asked Hashem to give Shabbos to his wine and fish, and of the Satmar Rav whose face burned while eating fish on Shabbos.

title.en: Two storekeepers whose Shabbos burned

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a young hidden tzaddik with a store, whose fiery kiddush puzzled his learned neighbor; he answered that while selling to the women he thought of Shabbos kiddush, while the neighbor at kiddush thought of the women he had watched. He then tells of Reb Nissan Pilchik in the Stoliner beis medrash, a peddler who blazed on Shabbos and, leaving a melaveh malkah at dawn, cheered another Jew that in six days it would be Shabbos.

title.en: How the Amoraim prepared; teshuvah and mikvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Rav Safra, Rav Huna and Rava stopped their learning to prepare for Shabbos with their own hands, the daily song that counts the days toward Shabbos, and Shammai who ate all week in honor of Shabbos. He concludes that one must prepare with teshuvah and immersion before Shabbos, reading 'Lev tahor' as a hint to tevilah, and adds that immersing on Shabbos morning is greater still.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos is a gift that comes with its own path, erev Shabbos, and describes how a Jew prepares for it with honor, mikveh, teshuvah, shame and longing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the outward honor of Shabbos: a white tablecloth, candles, silver vessels and Shabbos clothing, which leave a Shabbos grace in a Jewish home all week. The soul too needs clothing: the neshamah yeseirah must find a body made white through teshuvah, and so one goes to the mikveh on erev Shabbos with teshuvah. A kosher mikveh joins itself to rainwater from heaven, and so before Shabbos one connects to tzaddikim and their sefarim. He adds tevilah on Shabbos morning, before Nishmas, and tells how the Chida learned from the Rebbe Reb Elimelech that erev Shabbos is like Yom Kippur. From the Gemara that Shabbos is a gift and the halachah that a giver gives generously, including the path, he explains that erev Shabbos is the path to Shabbos, to be walked with Torah, teshuvah, shame and waiting, and he ends by urging the bachurim to attend the Friday night gatherings.

en: Honoring Shabbos with a white tablecloth, candles, silver and special clothing gives the Jewish home a Shabbos grace that remains all week.
The neshamah yeseirah must be received with a body made clean and white through teshuvah, which is why one goes to the mikveh on erev Shabbos with teshuvah.
Shabbos is a gift from Hashem, and one who gives a gift gives generously, including the path to it; erev Shabbos is that path.
Erev Shabbos is like Yom Kippur: one must do teshuvah, feel shame before the Ribono shel Olam for the week's failings, and enter Shabbos with that shame.
A Jew waits for Shabbos all week; 'shomer Shabbos' means one who waits for Shabbos.

title.en: The outward honor of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how a Jew honors Shabbos by tidying the house, covering the table with a white cloth, lighting candles and using silver candlesticks and a silver cup, and changing into Shabbos clothes as the Gemara teaches. This leaves a Shabbos grace on the Jewish home even in the middle of the week.

title.en: Teshuvah and the mikveh before Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the neshamah yeseirah must find a body made white through teshuvah, so one goes to the mikveh on erev Shabbos with teshuvah and immerses at least three times. He explains that a mikveh is full of holy names in its halachos and must come from rainwater from heaven, and that ordinary water becomes kosher by joining it; so too before Shabbos one connects to tzaddikim and their sefarim.

title.en: Shabbos-morning tevilah and Nishmas

summary.en: The Mashgiach says it is a great matter to immerse on Shabbos morning too, because a greater holiness comes down then, and the neshamah yeseirah of the morning comes at Nishmas. He brings the zemer Tzama Nafshi of Rabbi Avraham ibn Ezra, which longs for Nishmas, and says one can have in mind in the mikveh to merit a proper Nishmas.

title.en: Erev Shabbos as Yom Kippur: the Chida and the Rebbe Reb Elimelech

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from Ohr LaShamayim that erev Shabbos is like Yom Kippur and needs teshuvah. He tells how the Chida asked the Rebbe Reb Elimelech in heaven why his name caused a greater stir there, and the Rebbe Reb Elimelech answered that in his kitchen on erev Shabbos the women would ask one another forgiveness as on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Shabbos is a gift that includes the path

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk that Hashem 'gave' Shabbos and the Gemara that Shabbos is a good gift from His treasury. Citing the Chiddushei HaRim, he explains the halachah that a buyer of a pit must buy access to it while a recipient of a gift gets the path too, since a giver gives generously; so Hashem gave also the path to Shabbos, erev Shabbos, as seen from the double portion of manna on Friday.

title.en: Friday as a holy day of preparation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Friday is a holy day, criticizes bachurim who spend Friday playing ball, and says one prepares with a blatt Gemara, the mikveh and a chassidish sefer. He connects the sixth day and the sixth year to blessing, says Friday corresponds to Yosef HaTzaddik and holiness, and calls for teshuvah and shame before Hashem on erev Shabbos.

title.en: Shame, remembering and waiting for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that the word Bereishis holds 'yarei boshes' and that one enters Shabbos with shame. He says a Jew remembers and longs for Shabbos all week, from Motzei Shabbos on, cites the Rambam that one should prepare early on Friday and then sit and wait for Shabbos as for a great guest, and says each mitzvah of the week can be done with Shabbos in mind.

title.en: Shomer Shabbos, and the Friday night gatherings

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'shomer' as waiting, as with Yosef's dreams, so a shomer Shabbos is one who waits for Shabbos. He then stresses the Friday night and Shalosh Seudos gatherings with zemiros and talk of tzaddikim, urges the bachurim not to miss them, recalls the taste such a gathering left in him as a young man, and closes with Gut Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos is received by preparing for it all week and by being together with other Jews, and that Shabbos completes the 'seven notes' of creation, so that on Shabbos the day itself sings and a Jew must sing along with it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the teaching of the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov that a Jew longs for Shabbos all week, bringing Shammai, who ate all week in honor of Shabbos, and the Chasam Sofer's reading of 'lo seva'aru esh': light the fire at the start of the week. He then explains that Shabbos is received by being together with Jews: holiness is unity, and when Jews gather only their good combines, like small candles forming one great flame. Shabbos was meant to last forever before Adam's sin, so 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' speaks of the future day that is entirely Shabbos. Music has seven notes like the seven days; only with Shabbos is the 'piano' complete, which is why Kabbalas Shabbos sings Psalm 29 as its seventh chapter. On Shabbos the day itself sings, so Jews sing along: in davening, at the seudos and above all at shalosh seudos, whose real seudah is the singing.

en: A Jew prepares all week for Shabbos, through learning, davening and good deeds, so that he becomes a vessel for its holiness.
Holiness is unity and impurity is division; when Jews come together on Shabbos their good joins into one great good, while their faults do not combine.
Before Adam's sin the world was to be one endless Shabbos, and 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' speaks of that future day that is entirely Shabbos.
Music has seven notes because the world was created in seven days, each with its own note; with Shabbos, the seventh, the scale is complete and one can sing.
On weekdays the Levi'im sang the song of the day, but on Shabbos the day itself sings, so Jews must sing along with Shabbos in harmony.
The real seudah of shalosh seudos is the singing, eaten together with other Jews in the beis medrash.

title.en: Waiting for Shabbos all week

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov that a Jew longs for Shabbos all week, the Gemara about Shammai who ate all week in honor of Shabbos, and the Chasam Sofer's reading of 'lo seva'aru esh' as a call to kindle the fire from the start of the week.

title.en: Shabbos together with other Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a great way to receive Shabbos is to be together with Jews, citing Rav Yisroel of Vizhnitz. Each Jew has his own good; holiness is unity and evil is division, so when Jews gather their good joins like many small candles into one flame, while their faults do not.

title.en: Adam's endless Shabbos and the psalm of the future

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adam was placed in Gan Eden for a Shabbos that should never have ended, but the sin ended it; 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' therefore sings of the future day that is entirely Shabbos. He adds that on Friday night one praises Hashem more than all week, with the six chapters of Kabbalas Shabbos.

title.en: Seven notes and the seven days

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that music has seven notes because each day of creation has its own note, corresponding to the seven middos, with Shabbos as malchus. Only with the seventh is the 'piano' complete, which is why after the six chapters of Kabbalas Shabbos comes Psalm 29 with its seven 'kol Hashem', and then Lecha Dodi can be sung.

title.en: On Shabbos the day itself sings

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the song the Levi'im sang each day in the Beis Hamikdash and explains that on weekdays they sang, but on Shabbos the day itself sings. Therefore Jews must sing along with Shabbos in harmony, in davening, on Friday night and at shalosh seudos; this is the idea of zemiros.

title.en: Who really steers the world

summary.en: Going through Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos, the Mashgiach explains that the foolish do not see that the wicked flourish only to be destroyed, for Hashem runs the world. He tells of Rav Aharon Kotler and the car with a second steering wheel for a child, and explains 'tzaddik katamar yifrach' with the date palm and the cedar.

title.en: Zemiros, shalosh seudos and singing together

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that with the full seven notes Jews sing zemiros on Shabbos, together, above all at shalosh seudos in the beis medrash, where 'da hi seudasa' is said after eating and before singing because the singing is the real seudah. He closes with his shul's practice of giving the best seats near the chazzan to the bochurim so they sing and daven with fire together, like the malachim who give each other permission.

catalogTitle: “ויפח באפיו נשמת חיים.” נשמות ישראל עלו במחשבה. חילוקי מדריגות בנשמות ישראל.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's teaching that a Jewish soul is breathed from Hashem's innermost being and arose in His thought as the purpose of creation, and why, though all souls are one, there are endless levels among them.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 2: the second soul, unique to Jews, is a part of G-d above, as the Torah says Hashem 'breathed' a soul into Adam. Breath comes from within, so the soul comes from Hashem's inwardness, and every Jew says so of himself each morning. Every breath brings new life and a new task, which leads him to the story of the Alter Rebbe telling the Czar the time. He then explains that Jewish souls arose in Hashem's thought, the purpose for which the whole world was built, like a house built for the owner's wish to live in it, and compares this to a child that originates in the father's mind. After stressing that Hashem's wisdom is beyond human grasp, he asks how there can be levels among souls that are all one, and explains the levels through the structure of Adam HaRishon, the generations down to ikvesa diMeshicha, and the months down to Adar.

en: The Torah says Hashem 'breathed' the soul into Adam to teach that a Jewish soul comes from Hashem's innermost being, not from His 'hands', and this applies to every Jew.
Every breath is new life from Hashem, and every moment brings a different form of avodas Hashem.
Jewish souls arose in Hashem's thought first, and the entire universe was created only for their sake.
Hashem's wisdom is not a faculty He has, as it is in man; He is the knower and the knowledge, which the human mind was not made to grasp.
All Jewish souls are equal at their root; the differences are in their garments of Torah and mitzvos, and in the place each soul has in the structure of Adam HaRishon.
The generations descend from the dor hamidbar, the 'head', down to ikvesa diMeshicha, the 'heels', and the months descend in the same way down to Adar.

title.en: A soul breathed from within

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 2 on the second soul, unique to Jews, a part of G-d above, and explains why the Torah says Hashem 'breathed' a soul into Adam: breath comes from one's inwardness. He adds that every Jew says this of himself each morning and that every breath is new life from Hashem.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe tells the Czar the time

summary.en: Mentioning the Ba'al HaTanya's yahrzeit, the Mashgiach tells how the disguised Czar visited him in prison, how he recognized the king, and how he knew the exact time without a clock through the permutations of Hashem's Name that rule each hour, minute and second.

title.en: A new avodah in every moment

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws from the story that every moment calls for a different kind of avodas Hashem: with simchah at one time, with holding on to emunah at another. Life is dynamic, and with every breath a person takes in new life and a new shlichus.

title.en: Souls arose in His thought

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'the souls of Israel arose in thought' with the mashal of a man who builds a house: all the bricks and workers serve his first thought of living there. So the whole universe was created only because Hashem wanted Klal Yisrael, as the passuk calls Israel His firstborn son.

title.en: The Torah as the blueprint of nature

summary.en: In a digression the Mashgiach explains that Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world, so all of nature is in the Torah, and the great Chachamim learned medicine and the sciences from it. He contrasts this with scientists who only know the surface, illustrated by the question why a knife cuts challah and not the reverse.

title.en: Like a child from the father's mind

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's mashal: a child originates in the father's mind, which comes down and takes physical form, and so Jewish souls come from Hashem's thought, as the pesukim call Israel His son and children. He stresses that this is only a mashal, since Hashem's thought is not like ours, and that it applies to every individual Jew.

title.en: He is the knower and the knowledge

summary.en: Bringing Patach Eliyahu and the Rambam, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem's wisdom is not a faculty He has but is He Himself, which the human mind, made for this world like fins for water, cannot grasp. With the mashal of seeing a symphony he shows that the intellect is the wrong sense for this; only a deeper sense of emunah, and in prophets nevuah, reaches it.

title.en: If all are one, why levels?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks: if every Jew is a part of G-d above, and G-dliness is one and indivisible, how can there be higher and lower souls? He answers that at the root all are equal and the differences lie in their garments of Torah and mitzvos, as will be seen in the circle dance of the tzaddikim, and then reads the Tanya on the endless levels from the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu down to the generations before Moshiach.

title.en: Adam HaRishon, the challah of the world

summary.en: Pausing before going on, the Mashgiach explains that Adam HaRishon was the choice piece Hashem took from the 'dough' of the earth, from the place of the mizbeach, and so he is called the challah of the world. This is the reason he gives for the minhag the Rama records of women baking challah for Shabbos every Friday, since Chava brought death on him on a Friday, and in this 'challah' all Jewish souls are included.

title.en: Souls in the limbs of Adam HaRishon

summary.en: Citing a Medrash, the Mashgiach explains that every soul has its place in the body of Adam HaRishon: souls of the head are the thinkers and Talmidei Chachamim, like Moshe Rabbeinu; souls of the heart are the people of feeling and tefillah and the poets, like David HaMelech; then the hands and the feet. Every generation contains the whole structure, from its heads to its heels.

title.en: From the dor hamidbar to the heels

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in history too, the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu was the 'head' of Klal Yisrael, a gathering of heads, and the generations descend until ikvesa diMeshicha, the 'heels', which, like the sole of the foot, have little sensitivity to lofty feelings. He says this generation will be transformed into the head, and uses the mashal of a fern, whose every branch is a small copy of the whole.

title.en: Space, time and Adar's hiddenness

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same structure in space, where the earth has a head, heart and lower parts, and in time, where Nissan is the head of the months and Adar the lowest, the month of hester panim, as the Gemara finds Esther in 'I will surely hide My face' and the Megillah has no name of Hashem and no open miracles. Our era is the 'Adar' of history, and he returns to the Tanya's words on the souls of the Avos and of ikvesa diMeshicha, adding that each individual also contains different levels.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos, the seventh, is the day on which all of creation completes its song, and that Jews sing along with Shabbos in their zemiros and at seudos made holy by the presence of the Avos and of Shabbos itself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer: Hashem made seven days, seven lands and seven seas, and in each the seventh is the chosen one: Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael and the Kinneres. Music too has seven notes, and the Levi'im spent five years learning its wisdom. The Kinneres, the seventh sea, is named for the kinor, the harp, and is shaped like one; when the seven are complete the song begins. Through a story of the Stoliner patting the Blazhever Rav on the shoulder, he explains the passuk that the border 'touches the shoulder of Yam Kinneres'. Of all the Levi'im's daily psalms only Shabbos's is called 'a song', because Shabbos itself sings and Jews sing along with it. He speaks of the power of a niggun, of achdus in singing together, of preparing all week to feel Shabbos, of the holiness of Shabbos food, and of a Shabbos table where Shabbos itself is invited.

en: In each set of seven the seventh is the chosen one: Shabbos among days, Eretz Yisrael among lands, the Kinneres among seas.
The Kinneres is named for the kinor, a harp: once seven are complete, the song can begin.
Only the Levi'im's psalm for Shabbos opens with 'mizmor shir', because Shabbos itself sings, and Jews join its song.
The essence of a niggun is the unity of its notes, and Shabbos is the day of achdus, so Jews singing together at the table and at shalosh seudos is a great pleasure to Hashem.
A person who did not prepare and guard himself during the week cannot feel the taste of Shabbos.
Shabbos food is holy, and a Shabbos meal must invite the 'King', Shabbos itself, through divrei Torah, zemiros and holy conversation instead of weekday talk.

title.en: The seventh sea: why the Kinneres sings

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer on seven days, lands and seas, ties them to the seven notes of music that the Levi'im studied, and asks about the passuk on the border at Yam Kinneres. He explains that the Kinneres, the seventh sea, is named for the harp and shaped like one, and that Eretz Yisrael sings.

title.en: The Stoliner's pat on the shoulder

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Stoliner, after hearing the Blazhever Rav's holy kriyas haTorah, patted him on the shoulder so that he would daven Musaf. From this he explains the passuk: on Shabbos the border goes around Eretz Yisrael and pats the singing Kinneres on its shoulder.

title.en: Only Shabbos's psalm is a song

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the psalms the Levi'im sang each day and notes that only Shabbos's opens with 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos'. Shabbos itself sings, and since no person would dare sing to Hashem on his own, Jews sing along with Shabbos.

title.en: A day of song, and the power of a niggun

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Apter Rav that Shabbos is the time of singing, and a saying that one would sooner believe the seven seas dried up than that a Jew who can sing does not sing on Shabbos. He describes the singing of Friday night, the day meal and shalosh seudos, and explains that composing a true niggun takes a spirit close to ruach hakodesh.

title.en: Niggun as unity, Shabbos as achdus

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the niggunim of tzaddikim and of new composers sent down from Heaven, contrasting a real melody with a cat walking on a piano. The essence of a niggun is the unity of its notes; Shabbos is the secret of 'echad', so Jews singing zemiros together is a great pleasure to Hashem, and he laments those who leave before the zemiros.

title.en: Shalosh seudos and preparing for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions Yedid Nefesh and calls shalosh seudos the peak of Shabbos's achdus, as in 'Atah echad'. He explains that one who did not guard himself in holiness during the week cannot feel Shabbos, urges preparing from motzaei Shabbos, and contrasts those who daven Shabbos with sweetness with those who talk during davening.

title.en: The Avos at the seudos; holy Shabbos food

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Avos come to the Shabbos seudos of Jews united in achdus, and that Shabbos food contains holiness. He tells how Reb Dovid'l Biderman of Yerushalayim ate a spoiled cholent in Meron, saying one may not disgrace Shabbos food.

title.en: Inviting the King to the Shabbos table

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the day itself is the oneg, and brings a mashal of a man who prepared a feast for the king but never invited him. So a lavish Shabbos meal without calling in Shabbos is lacking; the table should hold divrei Torah, zemiros and stories of tzaddikim, not business talk.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach describes how people who strive higher keep Shabbos: guarding their speech, davening and learning at length, and reaching the peak of Shabbos at shalosh seudos with the zemer Bnei Heichala.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with speech on Shabbos: the kedushah of Shabbos limits a person's words to zemiros, brachos and Torah, and he should avoid talk that has no connection to Shabbos. He ties the three Shabbos meals to the Avos, with Friday night the meal of Yitzchak, and calls melave malka the meal of Dovid HaMelech. He discusses tefillas chatzos, a takanah and not an obligation, and tells of Rebbe Elimelech's melave malka. Since Hashem created the world with speech and rested on Shabbos, a higher person keeps Shabbos with his speech too, while still making the Shabbos table pleasant for his family. He then speaks of the long Shabbos davening, Torah learned on Shabbos, Shabbos as a bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, and the great ratzon of Shabbos afternoon. He closes with shalosh seudos: little eating, the Arizal's zemer Bnei Heichala sung with dveikus, the angels who come to look, and the forces of evil that cannot enter.

en: The kedushah of Shabbos limits speech: words of zemiros, brachos and Torah, and not talk that has no connection to Shabbos.
The Friday night meal is the meal of Yitzchak, the three Shabbos meals correspond to the Avos, and melave malka is the meal of Dovid HaMelech.
Because Hashem created the world with speech and rested on Shabbos, a higher person keeps Shabbos with his speech as well.
The Shabbos davening is longer, with many mizmorim not said during the week, and Torah learned on Shabbos is far higher than Torah learned during the week.
The high point of Shabbos is the afternoon, a time of great ratzon and rachamim.
At shalosh seudos one eats very little; its essence is the zemiros, above all Bnei Heichala, sung together with dveikus.

title.en: Speech on Shabbos and the Shabbos meals

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the kedushah of Shabbos limits speech to zemiros, brachos and words of holiness, and warns against talk unconnected to Shabbos. He ties the Friday night meal to Yitzchak, the three meals to the Avos, and melave malka to Dovid HaMelech.

title.en: Tefillas chatzos and Rebbe Elimelech's melave malka

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that tefillas chatzos is a takanah and not an obligation, since a great level cannot be made a duty, and calls it the tefillah of Dovid. He then tells how Rebbe Elimelech kept melave malka with only tea and instructed his children about it.

title.en: Higher people keep Shabbos with their speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that since the world was created with speech and Hashem rested on Shabbos, higher people refrain from idle words on Shabbos, yet must make a pleasant Shabbos table for their family. He brings the halachic side of not speaking about weekday work, the story of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's mother, and a reading of 'bechorish uvakatzir tishbos' as silence.

title.en: Tefillah and Torah on Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Divrei Emes that tefillah is the essence of Shabbos and describes the longer Shabbos davening with mizmorim not said during the week. He speaks of resting well so as to daven properly, of a fixed time for a chassidishe sefer, and of Torah learned on Shabbos being far higher than weekday Torah.

title.en: 'Between Me and Bnei Yisroel' and Shabbos afternoon

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Shabbos to the private talk of two close friends, a bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel. For the choshuve Yidden Shabbos is a yichud with Hashem, and its high point is the afternoon, a time of great ratzon unlike weekday mincha; he speaks of eating shalosh seudos together with a minyan.

title.en: Shalosh seudos and the Arizal's zemiros

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that at shalosh seudos one hardly eats and the essence is the zemiros, above all Bnei Heichala sung together with dveikus. He says the Arizal composed a zemer for each of the three meals, explains 'Bnei Heichala' as the King's palace children invited to eat with Him, and mentions the kabbalistic names of the meals, which he says he cannot explain.

title.en: Longing, angels and the closed door to evil

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the longing of shalosh seudos and how every small bite of the meal is precious. Angels come to see Jews sitting at shalosh seudos, the harsh judgments of weekday mincha are absent, and, as the zemer says, the brazen forces of evil cannot enter.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, through the image of an embryo whose hair and nails form last yet carry the same essence as the brain, the Tanya's teaching that even the lowest souls of Klal Yisrael stay bound with a wondrous bond to their first Source.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, the day Moshe Rabbeinu began to explain the Torah, and says every Jew who learns is joined to Moshe by a thread. Returning to Tanya chapter 2, he restates the question of how souls that are all a part of G-d can differ in level, both between people and within one person's nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah and yechidah. He builds the Tanya's answer on the development of a child: the brain forms first and the hair and nails last, after nine months, yet the same essence runs through all of them. So too some souls are near to Chochmah Ila'ah and some are as distant as the nails, yet all are bound to their root. He applies this to cutting nails before Shabbos, to the Mishnah on those without a share in the World to Come, to Achan and the word Yisrael, to the calendar where Adar and the heels of Moshiach are the hidden 'nails' of time, and finally to the Tanya's switch from 'madreigos' to the Aramaic 'dargin'.

en: Every soul of a Jew is a part of G-d, yet souls differ greatly in level, between people and within each person's five levels of soul.
In a child, the brain forms first and the hair and nails last, but all develop from the same drop and carry the same essence.
Some souls are close to the supernal Chochmah like the eyes to the brain, and some are as remote as the toenails, yet all remain bound to their first Source.
No Jew is ever truly cut off from Hashem; being cut off exists only in theory, as the 36 kerisos and the Mishnah on the World to Come show.
The heels of Moshiach, like the month of Adar, are the 'nails' of time: the most hidden and remote stage, just before the birth of the Geulah.
The Tanya's switch from the Hebrew 'madreigos' to the Aramaic 'dargin' shows that even souls sunk as low as Targum are still bound to their root.

title.en: Rosh Chodesh Shevat and Moshe's explaining

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rosh Chodesh Shevat, the day Moshe Rabbeinu began to explain the Torah in every language, and calls it a Rosh Hashanah of the tree of Torah when a new flow of Torah comes down. He says every Jew who learns is connected to Moshe by at least a thin thread.

title.en: How can souls differ in level?

summary.en: The Mashgiach restates the Tanya's question: if every soul is a part of G-d, who is one, how can there be great and small souls? He compares the separation to insulation around a live wire, then lists the five levels within a single soul, nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah and yechidah, and asks how there can be gradations among them too.

title.en: The embryo: brain first, hair and nails last

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's parable of a child's development from the father's drop: the brain forms first, the limbs after, and the hair and nails last, which is why the Gemara treats a child born with hair and nails as viable. He adds that the same chromosomes are found in the nails as in the brain, though the nails are removed from it by nine months.

title.en: Souls near and far from Chochmah Ila'ah

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the parable: souls come from the supernal Chochmah, the 'brain' of the Ribono shel Olam; the tzaddikim are the eyes, while other parts of Klal Yisrael are as remote as hair and nails, which can be cut off without being felt. He reads the Tanya's line that even the souls of the simplest Jews are drawn from the supernal brain and stay bound to it with a wondrous bond.

title.en: Nails from the father; no Jew is cut off

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the father contributes the white parts, including the nails, tracing them to the father's drop. He discusses cutting hair and nails before Shabbos, the Mishnah and Gemara on those with no share in the World to Come, and the 36 kerisos, concluding that being cut off is only theoretical and that cutting nails before Shabbos means shedding the foreign part of oneself.

title.en: Achan and the word Yisrael

summary.en: Asked about halachos for disposing of cut nails, the Mashgiach compares it to the Mishnah that only seems to sever some Jews. He brings Reb Tzadok on Achan: the Gemara lists his sins, yet 'even though he sinned he is Yisrael', and Yisrael, the last word of the Torah, is bound to Bereishis, its first. He then brings the Sefer Yetzirah that the world was made in place, time and soul, and traces Klal Yisrael from Moshe's generation to the heels of Moshiach.

title.en: Adar and the heels of Moshiach in time

summary.en: The Mashgiach carries the pattern into time: Nisan corresponds to Moshe and the generation of the desert, and Adar, the last month, has no open miracles and the Megillah never names Hashem. He explains that the Megillah was written at the heels of the Babylonian exile, when even Daniel miscalculated the 70 years, because a time of test is a time of hidden face, and he calls the heels of Moshiach the nails of the calendar and the birth pangs before the Geulah.

title.en: From 'madreigos' to 'dargin'; Yaakov and Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Tanya opens with 'madreigos' and ends with the Aramaic 'dargin', and brings the Arizal that tardeimah, Adam's deep sleep, equals Targum in gematria: the end of the exile is a deep sleep far from the brain, the realm of Targum and kelipah. He concludes that even these lowest levels are bound to their root, as shown by the names Yaakov, with its heel, and Yisrael, with its rosh and with the largest and smallest letters.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why shalosh seudos is the 'will of all wills', a time beyond time and without boundaries, and moves from there to Shabbos as a source of forgiveness and to the power of kiddush.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to the three seudos of Shabbos and focuses on shalosh seudos. It is called raava d'raavin, the will of wills: all of Shabbos is a time of favor, and from mincha on comes a still greater et ratzon. A Jew should then awaken a strong desire to become upright, and even one who feels nothing gains by sitting with friends in love. Time and place are created things; before creation Hashem had a will to create, and shalosh seudos, before the first Sunday, stands above time. He demands seriousness at the table and tells of the Rebbe of Rimanov who once pushed a man for chatting then. Shalosh seudos, a boundless inheritance of Yaakov, extends past the end of Shabbos. He then speaks of Shabbos atoning for sin, the need to learn its halachos, the angels' blessing, teshuvah before kiddush, and the Satmar Rav's kiddush.

en: Shalosh seudos is called raava d'raavin because all of Shabbos is a time of favor, and from mincha a still greater et ratzon begins, a will within the will.
At shalosh seudos a Jew should arouse a great desire to become upright from now on, and if he cannot, he should at least want to have that desire.
Shalosh seudos stands above time: it corresponds to the moment before creation when Hashem willed to create the world, so it is a time to will to be created anew as an upright Jew.
Shalosh seudos is a boundless inheritance like Yaakov's, so its holiness continues for those still sitting at it after the time of Shabbos has passed.
Shabbos kept properly brings forgiveness of sins, but one cannot be a shomer Shabbos without learning the halachos of Shabbos.
Kiddush is testimony that Hashem created the world, so the Bnei Yissaschar says to do teshuvah before kiddush, and it must be said or heard with great kavanah.

title.en: Shalosh seudos as raava d'raavin

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the three seudos correspond to the tefillos of Shabbos, says that shalosh seudos is a time for words of Torah and not idle talk, and explains why it is called the will of wills. He says a Jew should then resolve to become upright, or at least want to want it.

title.en: When one feels nothing: sitting with friends

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares a Shabbos without feeling to Avraham at the Akeidah, who saw the place from afar yet served with acceptance of the yoke. He explains that sitting at shalosh seudos with friends in love, like the angels who receive from one another, lets even one without enthusiasm absorb it, as standing near a tzaddik helps in davening.

title.en: Shalosh seudos is above time

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that time and place are created things, bringing the Gemara that the aron took up no space. Before creation there was no time, only Hashem's will to create; shalosh seudos, before the world's first day, is that time above time, so a Jew can then will to be created anew, and it is a great time for yeshuos, especially with a minyan.

title.en: Seriousness at shalosh seudos; the Rimanov story

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks that people sit seriously and not chat while waiting for shalosh seudos, using the minutes for Tehillim or a sefer. He tells of the Rebbe of Rimanov, who never bothered a Jew except once, when he pushed a man chatting at shalosh seudos, because it is a holy time.

title.en: Shalosh seudos extends Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the name 'shalosh seudos' means it includes all three meals, and that its et ratzon lasts past bentching and even past the time, so for those still sitting it is still Shabbos. This benefits souls released from Gehinnom on Shabbos; he notes two views in the seforim on how this works.

title.en: Torah after the time; Yaakov's boundless inheritance

summary.en: The Mashgiach says tzaddikim teach that divrei Torah at shalosh seudos should be said after the time, when the et ratzon is greater. He explains that Avraham and Yitzchak were promised Eretz Yisrael with borders, but Yaakov was promised that he would spread out in every direction, a nachalah without boundaries; shalosh seudos is Yaakov's inheritance, so the clock cannot end it.

title.en: Shabbos, forgiveness and teshuvah before kiddush

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one who keeps Shabbos properly is forgiven even for idolatry, and stresses that being a shomer Shabbos requires learning its halachos, at least in Kitzur Shulchan Aruch before Mishnah Berurah. He brings the Gemara of the two angels who bless one who says Vayechulu, the dispute of the Maharal and the Taz whether teshuvah is needed, and the Bnei Yissaschar that one should do teshuvah before kiddush, since kiddush is testimony and a rasha cannot testify.

title.en: Kiddush with kavanah; the Satmar Rav's kiddush

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells children to say or follow kiddush in a siddur with great kavanah, and describes hearing the Satmar Rav's kiddush, when the whole beis medrash seemed to testify to creation, and the gathering of tzaddikim in Williamsburg after the war. He ends with a tzaddik who told people needing a yeshuah to come before kiddush, since one who says Vayechulu becomes a partner in creation, and closes the series on Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the first parsha of tefillin speaks only of a 'remembrance' while the later ones speak of 'totafos', and shows how a bar mitzvah is a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim in which the boy adds to the beauty of Hashem's own tefillin.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by linking the bar mitzvah with tefillin, then notes that the parsha of Kadesh calls tefillin a 'remembrance between your eyes', while the other parshiyos say 'totafos'. He gives two answers. The first parsha speaks of Pesach, when tefillin are not worn, so it is only a remembrance, as Chazal explain 'zichron teruah' of a Rosh Hashanah on Shabbos. And, from the Imrei Emes, in the desert the Jews had only the first two parshiyos, while 'totafos' means four. He explains tefillin as attachment to Hashem and the bar mitzvah as a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim, tells of Reb Dovid'l of Tolna leaving his boyhood games, and teaches that the boy must know his worth as Hashem's firstborn, add to the beauty of Hashem's tefillin, and search himself by the light of Torah as he enters his fourteenth year. He closes with a brachah.

en: The first parsha of tefillin calls them only a 'remembrance' because it speaks of Pesach, when tefillin are not worn.
Following the Imrei Emes, in the desert the Jews wore tefillin with only the first two parshiyos, so the first parsha could not yet say 'totafos', which means four parshiyos.
Tefillin express a Jew's attachment to Hashem, and a bar mitzvah is a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim, leaving childish, yetzer-hara things for the service of Hashem.
A bar mitzvah boy must know how precious he is to Hashem, as Hashem's firstborn.
Hashem's tefillin speak of the beauty of the Jewish people, and the bar mitzvah boy must add to that beauty.
Entering his fourteenth year, the boy must search himself by the light of Torah for any 'chametz' that needs to be cleared out.

He answers that the first parsha speaks of Pesach, when tefillin are not worn, and then, from the Imrei Emes, that in the desert the Jews had only the first two parshiyos, while 'totafos' means four.

title.en: Bar mitzvah as a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains tefillin as attachment to Hashem and the bar mitzvah as leaving childish things for the service of Hashem, tells how Reb Dovid'l of Tolna took leave of his boyhood play at his bar mitzvah, and from the parsha of Kadesh li chol bechor teaches that the boy must know he is precious to Hashem.

title.en: Adding to Hashem's tefillin; the fourteenth year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem's tefillin speak of the beauty of the Jewish people and that the boy must add to it, applies 'Or l'arba'ah asar bodkin es hachametz' to entering the fourteenth year, calls the first year after bar mitzvah the firstborn of a whole life, and closes with a brachah for the boy, his family and the final redemption.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a bris in the week of Parshas Ki Savo, the sixth week of consolation and the week of the middah of yesod, is a good sign, since the avodah of that week, like the bris, is to remove the orlah and reveal the good hidden in every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the verse calling the curses of Ki Savo 'the words of the covenant', and explains that the tochachah's harsh words are vessels of blessing that must be uncovered. That uncovering is bris milah: every Jew has good in him, and his avodah, beginning with the bris, is to remove the orlah covering it. Ki Savo is the sixth of the seven weeks of consolation, the week of yesod, the middah of the bris, and its avodah is to reveal that good. So too is Elul's avodah, hinted in the verse about the circumcision of the heart whose initials spell Elul. The haftorah's words about the nations he compares to milah and periah, and it ends with 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim'. A bris in this week is therefore a good sign, and he blesses the child, the family and Klal Yisrael.

en: The Mashgiach says the curses of Ki Savo, called 'the words of the covenant', are in truth vessels of blessing that need to be uncovered.
Every Jew has good in him, and his avodah, beginning with bris milah, is to remove the orlah that covers it.
Parshas Ki Savo is the sixth of the seven weeks of consolation, corresponding to the middah of bris, yesod, and its avodah is to reveal the good.
The avodah of Elul is the circumcision of the heart, as hinted in the verse whose initials spell Elul.
A bris in the sixth week, the week of 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim', is a good sign that the child will be a tzaddik.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that just as the lowest soul, the month of Adar and the hidden story of the Megillah still hold Hashem's full presence, the light that descends through the four worlds remains bound to its Source.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's image of the soul descending like a seed from the father's brain to the toenails, which still carry its essence, and applies it, following the Sefer Yetzirah, to space, time and soul. In time, Nisan is the month of open miracles and Adar the last month, like our generation at the heels of Moshiach: a time of hester panim. Adar comes from 'aderes', a cloak; Hashem is there but hidden. In the Megillah His name is absent and 'HaMelech' stands for Him, because Amalek conceals the Name, as shown by Rashi on 'kes Kah' and by gematria. The Megillah trains a person to see hidden miracles, even in the daily news, and to find Hashem's name between the lines. He then explains the four worlds of Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, and the Tanya's answer that even the lowest Jew remains bound to the Source.

en: The soul descends level by level like a seed that develops down to the toenails, yet the essence of the source remains even in the lowest part.
Following the Sefer Yetzirah, the same pattern appears in space, time and soul, with a Kodesh HaKodashim in each.
Adar, the last month, and our generation, the heels of Moshiach, are times of hester panim in which Hashem is present but unseen.
In the Megillah Hashem's name is hidden behind 'HaMelech' because Amalek conceals the Name and the Throne.
The Megillah is an exercise in reading between the lines to see hidden miracles and Hashem's hand in all events.
Hashem's light descended through the four worlds, Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, so that the creations could bear it.
Even the lowest Jew is truly a part of G-d above, bound to the Source and drawing his life through the tzaddikim of his generation.

Amalek and the incomplete Divine name

title.en: The soul's descent in space, time and soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews how the soul comes down like a seed developing from the head to the toenails, which still carry its essence. He brings the Sefer Yetzirah that space, time and soul mirror each other, and shows the Kodesh HaKodashim in each, meeting when the Kohen Gadol enters on Yom Kippur.

title.en: From Nisan to Adar, from Sinai to our generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in time Nisan is the beginning, the month of open miracles, while Adar is the last month, like our generation at the heels of Moshiach. In both there is hester panim, Hashem's name is not seen, and what remains are questions on Hashem.

title.en: Adar as a cloak; the miracle of survival

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the questions after the Holocaust to the questions of the Jews in Haman's time, and explains that Adar comes from 'aderes', a cloak: Hashem is as present as in Nisan, only hidden. He says the very survival of Klal Yisrael among the nations, and its revival after the Holocaust, is the greatest miracle for one who opens his eyes.

title.en: HaMelech in the Megillah, and Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Megillah reads like a story without miracles or Hashem's name, yet 'HaMelech' refers to Hashem, who uses Achashverosh as His tool. He explains that the Name is hidden because of Amalek, bringing Rashi on 'kes Kah', and shows that HaMelech, Haman and 'kes Kah' each equal 95, while 'macho emcheh' equals the 107 of the completed Throne and Name.

title.en: Seeing the hidden hand: the medicine parable

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a dying man for whom both the rare medicine and the one doctor who can give it arrive by ship within minutes, showing that perfect timing reveals Hashem's direction, as in the Megillah. He adds that rain, crops and the news are all miracles directed from Heaven, and that a person must train himself to see this hashgachah pratis.

title.en: Hashem's name between the lines of the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who sees the miracles can make the brachah on the Megillah, and that at every turning point Hashem's four-letter name appears in the initial or final letters of a phrase. He shows it in Haman's words 'zeh einenu shoveh li', with the letters reversed for strict judgment, and in Esther's 'yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom', in order for kindness.

title.en: From the Megillah back to the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that one who has learned to read the Megillah can see Hashem in the daily newspaper, and that with Moshiach the whole galus will be seen as one plan. He returns to the Tanya: the worst Jew is a part of G-d above just like the greatest tzaddik, only covered by sins, while tzaddikim are in contact with their soul and have ruach hakodesh.

title.en: The four worlds and the light of creation

summary.en: Reading 'v'kacha mamash' in the Tanya, the Mashgiach introduces the four worlds of the Kabbalah seforim. He explains that Hashem emanated a 'light', the least physical word available, and reduced it step by step into Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, down to our universe.

title.en: What the names of the worlds mean

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that because the world was created with loshon hakodesh, each Hebrew word describes its essence, as Adam HaRishon named the creatures. Atzilus comes from 'etzel', closest to Hashem; 'olam' from 'ne'elam', hidden; Beriah is creation from nothing; Yetzirah is forming. The light passed through these stages so that we can bear it, like viewing the sun through dark films.

title.en: The Tanya's answer: all are bound to the Source

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that the souls, down to the lowest, remain bound in a wondrous unity with the extension of Hashem's chochmah. This answers the question at the start of the perek about differing levels among Jews: like toenails, all share one essence that grew coarser, and the lowest Jew draws his life through the greatest tzaddik of the generation. He closes with the parable of electric current reduced through ever thinner wires.

catalogTitle: בר מצוה: bar mitzva Chaya Surah

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Jewish kiddushin is learned from the purchase of Me'aras HaMachpelah: a Jewish marriage is a bond of souls that outlives the body, and a bar mitzvah, when a boy receives his soul and the Torah as his kallah, is a wedding of the same kind.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Me'aras HaMachpelah, through which, the Midrashim say, Jewish prayers and souls pass. The Gemara learns that a woman is betrothed with money from Avraham's purchase of the cave from Efron. He asks why the happiest moment of life should be learned from a grave, and answers that Avraham wanted his bond with Sarah to continue beyond life: a Jewish marriage is a union of souls that existed before birth and outlasts the body. He then brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah is like a wedding: the boy receives his soul, and the Torah, given as a kallah and an inheritance of all Jews, becomes his. Through the Chasam Sofer on Haman he shows that the Torah lives in every Jew. Finally he contrasts Efron's dust with the fire of zrizus the Torah needs, and blesses the boy, noting that the holy ancestors attend the simcha.

en: The Mashgiach says, citing the Midrashim, that Jewish prayers and souls pass through Me'aras HaMachpelah on their way up.
Kiddushin with money is learned from Avraham's purchase of the cave, because a Jewish marriage is a bond of souls that continues even after death.
A couple's souls were joined even before they were born, so every Jewish marriage is a union of souls.
A bar mitzvah is like a wedding: the boy receives his soul, which is Torah, and the Torah becomes betrothed to him as a kallah.
The Torah is the inheritance of every Jew and lies in his inner self even if he is not a talmid chacham.
Torah must be served with zrizus, the fire that rises, in contrast to the dust of Efron that brings sadness.

title.en: Kiddushin learned from the Machpelah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Me'aras HaMachpelah as the gate of prayers and souls, notes that kiddushin with money is learned from its purchase, and asks why a wedding should be learned from a grave. He answers that Avraham wanted his bond with Sarah to continue beyond life, since a Jewish marriage is a union of souls that existed before birth.

title.en: The bar mitzvah as a wedding with the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah should be celebrated like a wedding, since the boy then receives his soul, which is Torah, and tells how Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai married off his son the night he turned thirteen. Through 'morasha kehillas Yaakov' and the Chasam Sofer on Haman he shows that the Torah is the inheritance and kallah of every Jew.

title.en: Efron's dust and the fire of zrizus

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the bar mitzvah to the parsha: Efron was a klipah in Chevron blocking the way to the Machpelah, and Avraham overcame it. Building on the father's words about the name Naftali Tzvi, he contrasts the fire of zrizus with the dust of Efron and sadness, then says the holy ancestors attend the simcha and blesses the boy.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Elul, the Mashgiach explains that the curses of Parshas Ki Savo hold hidden blessings, just as the bris removes the orlah to reveal the inner holiness of a Jew, and that a father's bris is done purely for the sake of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the question of the Zera Kodesh: Parshas Bechukosai ends its curses with consolation, while Parshas Ki Savo ends with curses alone. He notes that at Har Gerizim and Har Eival only the curses are written, and the Gemara learns the blessings from them by a hekesh. He explains that great good is hidden in the Torah, covered by an orlah, and the bris reveals the inner point. Elul, hinted in 'umal Hashem es levavcha', is the milah of the year, when Tamuz and Av are revealed as good; this is why Ki Savo is read then. The passuk itself answers: 'these are the words of the bris'. He links the bris to the completion of the child's formation and to Avraham Avinu, and contrasts it with Torah and chuppah, where other motives can enter. A bris is purely for Heaven, and he blesses the child accordingly.

en: Only the curses of Har Eival are written in Ki Savo; the blessings are learned from them by a hekesh, a sign that the blessings are contained within the curses.
Great good is hidden in the Torah under a covering like an orlah; when the orlah is removed, as at a bris, the inner point is revealed.
Elul, hinted in 'umal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha ve'es levav zarecha', is the bris milah of the year, when the hard months of Tamuz and Av are revealed as good.
The bris completes the formation of the child that began nine months earlier, just as Avraham Avinu with his bris was the completion of creation.
Unlike teaching Torah or arranging a chuppah, where other motives can enter, a father makes a bris purely for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: Curses without consolation, and the hidden good

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zera Kodesh's wonder that Ki Savo, unlike Bechukosai, ends without consolation, and notes that only the curses are written while the Gemara learns the blessings from them. He explains that great good lies hidden under an orlah, and that the bris reveals Hashem's covenant with every Jew and the inner point that no place is empty of Him.

title.en: Blessings inside the curses; Elul as the bris of the year

summary.en: Using the hekesh and a rule of Tosafos in Zevachim, the Mashgiach shows that the blessings are contained in the curses. He then explains that Ki Savo is read in Elul because Elul is the milah of the year, hinted in 'umal Hashem', when Tamuz and Av are revealed as good, and compares this to the bris completing a child's formation.

title.en: 'These are the words of the bris' and Avraham Avinu

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the opening question from the passuk 'eleh divrei habris': the curses are words of the bris, which reveals the inner point. He ties this to the end of the year, to the passuk 'umal Hashem' addressed to the generation of Moshiach and to 'levav zarecha', and to Avraham Avinu, whose holiness flares up at every bris and passes from father to child.

title.en: A bris purely for Heaven, and the blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's list of a father's duties to his son and contrasts Torah study and chuppah, where other motives can enter, as with Elisha ben Avuya's father, with the bris, which a father does with no motive but bringing his child into the covenant of Avraham. He closes with the blessing that just as the child entered the bris, so may he enter into Torah, chuppah and good deeds.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in the week of Toldos, the Mashgiach contrasts Yaakov's 'today' of Torah and mitzvos with Esav's 'today' of grabbing pleasure, describes the bar mitzvah as the boy's wedding with the Torah attended by his holy ancestors, and calls Toldos, the sixth sedra, a parsha of brachos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Yaakov's words to Esav, 'sell me as of today your birthright', and describes two opposite ways of life. The upright Jew's 'today' is 'today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward': Torah and good deeds now, reward later. The rasha's 'today' is 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die': grab the world now. Yaakov told Esav that their 'todays' differ, and Esav answered that he was going to die, so what was the birthright to him. Turning to the bar mitzvah, the Mashgiach says the boy accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos, and brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah is celebrated like a wedding, since the boy becomes a chassan to the Torah. His holy ancestors come to the simcha, so it must be taken seriously. He speaks of the gifts Hashem gives a bar mitzvah boy, notes that Toldos is a sedra of brachos, and blesses the boy.

en: The Mashgiach describes two opposite views of 'today': the upright Jew's, of doing mitzvos now and receiving reward later, and the rasha's, of grabbing pleasure now.
Yaakov's 'as of today' to Esav expresses that their two 'todays' are opposed.
At bar mitzvah a boy accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos and becomes a chassan to the holy Torah, so the simcha is like a wedding.
The holy ancestors come to a child's simcha, so a bar mitzvah must be treated as a holy occasion, not merely a party.
Toldos is a sedra of brachos and the sixth sedra, which the Mashgiach associates with yesod, the foundation of bracha.

title.en: Two kinds of 'today'

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'sell me as of today your birthright' and contrasts the upright Jew's 'today to do them, tomorrow their reward' with the rasha's 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'. He then turns to the bar mitzvah boy, who accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos and should be a source of nachas.

title.en: A wedding with the Torah, attended by ancestors

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that a father must celebrate his son's bar mitzvah like a wedding, since the boy becomes a chassan to the Torah, and the holy sefarim that parents and grandparents come from Gan Eden to a child's simcha. Since the boy descends from great tzaddikim, the simcha is a holy occasion and not merely a party.

title.en: Gifts from Hashem and a sedra of brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the custom of giving gifts at a bar mitzvah and says that above all Hashem should give the boy purity of soul and a desire for mitzvos. He notes that Toldos, the sixth sedra, is full of brachos, calls this a good sign, and blesses the boy to become a masmid and a gadol baTorah.

oneLiner.en: On the opening of Tanya chapter three, the Mashgiach explains that the ten utterances of creation are the ten sefiros through which Hashem reveals Himself, and that a person carries them as intellect (Chabad) and seven character traits (Chagas Nehim).

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter three: each of nefesh, ruach and neshamah contains ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefiros. He starts from the Mishnah's ten utterances of creation and the Gemara's question that only nine are found, and explains that these ten are ten powers, the sefiros, through which the infinite Hashem appears to us, filtered down through the worlds like sunlight through darkened films. Man, created in the image of G-d, contains all ten, though in him they are not called sefiros but Chabad (intellect) and seven midos. He defines chesed as giving and extending, gevurah as fear and withdrawal, tiferes as a new harmony, netzach and hod as two ways of survival, yesod as the power to create. He links the seven midos to music, the seven days of creation and Shabbos, contrasts Chabad's path of intellect with other Chassidim's path of emotion, and shows that the seven midos can serve good or evil, unlike the higher three.

en: The ten utterances of creation are ten powers, the sefiros, through which the infinite Hashem reveals Himself in creation in different aspects.
Man, created in the image of G-d, contains all ten, but in him they are not called sefiros; they are divided into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim.
Chesed is extending oneself and giving; gevurah is fear and drawing into oneself; tiferes is the harmony that arises when the two meet.
Netzach and hod are two ways of survival, fighting the adversary or bending under pressure; yesod is the power to create.
Chabad, the intellect, is the father and root of the midos and is above this world, so in essence it has no evil, while the seven midos can be used for good or for evil.
Chesed and gevurah run through all of creation: male and female, summer and winter, the poles of a magnet, day and night.
