title.en: Tanya chapter three and the ten utterances

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter three and recalls that nefesh, ruach and neshamah each consist of ten powers. He brings the Mishnah's ten utterances of creation, the Gemara's question that only nine are found and its answers, and explains that these ten are the sefiros through which the infinite Hashem appears in creation.

title.en: From the sefiros above to man below

summary.en: With the mashal of looking at the sun through darkened films, the Mashgiach describes how the light comes down from Atzilus to Asiyah. Man, in the image of G-d, contains the ten, but in him they are not called sefiros; the Mashgiach shows that Adam equals the filled-out Name of Havayah and divides the ten into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim.

title.en: Chesed and gevurah: giving and withdrawing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chabad belongs only to man while midos are found even in animals. Chesed is love that extends itself and gives; gevurah is fear, a contraction into oneself. He applies this to the male as giver and the female as receiver, as seen in kiddushin and the kesubah.

title.en: Tiferes: a new harmony, not a mixture

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains tiferes as the blending of chesed and gevurah, tied to the joining of mercy at the start of Bereishis and to the last utterance about a helpmate. With lemonade, a painting, a niggun and a second voice harmonizing, he shows that tiferes is a qualitatively new creation, and applies it to man and woman together.

title.en: Netzach, hod, yesod and the body

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines netzach as surviving by fighting and hod as surviving by yielding. He brings Pasach Eliyahu from the Tikkunei Zohar, which maps the sefiros onto the body: chesed the right arm, gevurah the left, tiferes the body, netzach and hod the two legs, yesod the organ of creation and malchus the mouth, and postpones explaining malchus.

title.en: Music, the days of creation and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the seven sefiros to the seven notes of music, brings the harp of seven, eight and ten strings, and the Zohar's heichal opened only by song. Each day of creation was made with one sefira; when Shabbos completes the harp, one can sing zemiros, and the seven voices of the psalm said to welcome Shabbos correspond to the sefiros.

title.en: Chabad: the mochin and the Chabad derech

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that chochmah, binah and da'as are mochin, the father, mother and root of the midos. He explains the name Chabad Chassidus: serving Hashem through understanding creation, while most other Chassidim worked on love, fear and praise of Hashem and were wary of delving into what is above this world.

title.en: Animals have one trait, man has all

summary.en: Everything in creation comes from one or a combination of the ten. Each animal shows one sefira, like the lion, whose name equals gevurah, or the timid sheep, while man, to whom every part of creation contributed according to the Ramban, can be anything, with one or two sefiros dominant.

title.en: The seven midos for good and for evil

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the upper three are above this world and have no evil, while the seven lower midos, where the Tree of Knowledge took hold, can be good or bad. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on the passuk calling a forbidden union chesed, a judge who fears the powerful, and poetry that inflames the yetzer, and adds that the ten sons of Haman are the ten sefiros of impurity.

title.en: Chesed and gevurah in all creation; the Tanya's words

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows chesed and gevurah throughout creation: male and female, summer and winter, positive and negative charge, the poles of a magnet pointing north and south, day and night. He then reads the Tanya's words that each level contains ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefiros, divided into three mothers and seven doubles, and closes with intellect and midos in the human soul.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Elul, the Mashgiach ties the mitzvah of milah to the month through the passuk in Nitzavim "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha v'es levav", and closes with blessings for the child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk from parshas Nitzavim, "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha v'es levav zar'echa", a passuk about milah of the heart, and connects it to the month of Elul; he speaks of a series of pesukim tied to Elul, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li". He describes the days of Elul, from Rosh Chodesh on, as a preparation for Rosh Hashanah, the time that sets the whole year. He returns to the passuk of milah and says this bris took place at an auspicious time, when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused. He ends with blessings that the child grow up to bring nachas to his family and to Klal Yisroel and be dear before the Ribono shel Olam.

en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Nitzavim, "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha", in connection with the bris.
He speaks of a series of pesukim that are connected to Elul, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li".
The days of Elul lead up to Rosh Hashanah, the time that sets the whole year.
The bris took place at a good time, when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused.
He blesses the child to grow up and bring nachas to his family and to Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The passuk of milah and the month of Elul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Nitzavim "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha" and ties it to Elul, mentioning a series of pesukim connected to the month, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li". He describes Elul as the lead-up to Rosh Hashanah, which sets the whole year.

title.en: A bris in the days of rachamim; blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the passuk of milah and says this bris came at an auspicious time, when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused. He blesses the child to grow up to bring nachas to his family and to Klal Yisroel.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah, the Mashgiach explains through the Shem MiShmuel why "a new king arose over Egypt" when milah was neglected, and teaches that tefillin, which open with "kadesh li kol bechor", bring the bar mitzvah and everyone present a daily renewal in avodas Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Shem MiShmuel, who brings a Midrash linking "a new king arose over Egypt" to the Jews there not keeping milah, and asks what the connection is. He first brings the Avnei Nezer on a Midrash about Achashverosh's feast: when the Jews did not keep Shabbos, a gift from the Ribono shel Olam, the sitra achra seized its oneg, and that was the feast. The Shem MiShmuel says milah brings chiyus and freshness; when the Jews neglected it, Pharaoh seized the "chadash". So too a bar mitzvah receives tefillin, which begin with "kadesh li kol bechor": a bechor means newness, and tefillin should renew a person's avodas Hashem every day. The Mashgiach contrasts weekday tefillin with Shabbos tefillin, explains that guests at a bar mitzvah gain renewal and so take back what the new king seized, and closes with blessings.

en: According to the Avnei Nezer, when the Jews did not keep Shabbos, the sitra achra seized its oneg, and this was Achashverosh's feast.
The Shem MiShmuel says milah brings chiyus and freshness; when it was neglected in Egypt, Pharaoh seized the newness, as "a new king arose".
Tefillin open with "kadesh li kol bechor", and bechor means something new; tefillin should give renewal in avodas Hashem every day.
Of all the mitzvos a bar mitzvah becomes obligated in, the main one is tefillin, and the seudah is on account of the tefillin.
Guests at a bar mitzvah recall their own bar mitzvah and gain renewal, taking back what the new king of Egypt seized.

title.en: Why "a new king" arose when milah was neglected

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shem MiShmuel's question on the Midrash linking "a new king arose over Egypt" to the neglect of milah. Through the Avnei Nezer on Achashverosh's feast he explains that a gift of Hashem left unused is seized by the sitra achra, and so Pharaoh seized the freshness that milah brings.

title.en: Tefillin and renewal at a bar mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a bar mitzvah receives tefillin, which open with "kadesh li kol bechor", a call to daily renewal in avodas Hashem. He contrasts weekday and Shabbos tefillin, says the guests too gain renewal and take back what the new king seized, and blesses the bar mitzvah and all present.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, the Mashgiach explains that these days and the mitzvah of milah both lift a Jew above nature, drawing down the thirteen middos of rachamim upon Klal Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah: their avodah is not according to nature, and a Jew escapes from what is "under the sun" to a place above nature. He brings Barchi Nafshi, where Dovid HaMelech describes the order of nature: at night the animals rule, by day man goes out to his work. In these days a Jew rises at night, against that order. The ten days correspond to the ten maamaros, and the tenth, Yom Kippur, corresponds to "lachem yihyeh l'ochlah", the maamar of eating, yet on that very day a Jew rises above nature. Above the sun there is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos that no sin reaches. According to the Maharal, milah is on the eighth day because eight is above the seven days of creation; milah too is above nature, and its thirteen brisos draw down the thirteen middos. The child, named after the Gerrer Rebbe, is a sign of yeshuos, and the Mashgiach closes with blessings.

en: The avodah of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah is above nature: a Jew escapes from what is "under the sun".
Barchi Nafshi describes nature's order, in which man sleeps at night and works by day; in these days a Jew rises at night against that order.
Yom Kippur, the tenth day, corresponds to the tenth maamar, "lachem yihyeh l'ochlah", yet on it a Jew rises above the nature of eating.
Above nature there is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos that no sin reaches.
According to the Maharal, milah is on the eighth day because eight is above the seven days of creation, and milah is above nature.
The thirteen brisos of milah correspond to the thirteen middos and draw down rachamim upon Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Rising above nature in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the avodah of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah is above nature. He brings Barchi Nafshi's order of night and day, and explains that the ten days correspond to the ten maamaros, so that Yom Kippur matches the maamar of eating, yet on it a Jew rises above nature.

title.en: Milah above nature; blessings for the child

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that above the sun is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos. He brings the Maharal that milah, on the eighth day, is above nature, and says its thirteen brisos draw down the thirteen middos; the child, named after the Gerrer Rebbe, is a good sign for Klal Yisroel in these days. He closes by blessing the child to bring nachas to his parents, to Klal Yisroel and to the Ribono shel Olam, and wishes all a gmar chasimah tovah.

catalogTitle: ג' ראשונות' ז' תחתונות. העשר מכות נמשכים מהעשרה מאמרות' ונתגלה אח"כ בעשרת הדברות. (התחדשות של ניסן -קדושת המצות)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows how the Asarah Maamaros of creation were revealed through the Ten Makkos and given in the Aseres Hadibros, and how Nissan, the month of renewal and of emunah, and its matzah call on a person to renew himself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the three upper and seven lower levels, which become more tangible as they descend into the world. Hashem created the world with the Asarah Maamaros, but no one saw it; through the Ten Makkos He showed that every part of creation is His, against idolatry and against philosophers who say He left the world to run by itself. The makkos went in reverse order, from earthly to heavenly, and the Torah, through the Aseres Hadibros, then contained it all. He turns to Nissan, the reishis of the year, when the world was actually created and everything is renewed, and says a person should renew himself in avodas Hashem. Avraham, the first Jew, gave the mitzvah of emunah, and matzah is the food of emunah. Man contains all ten traits, so bread is his food; matzah, three times forty-five, stands higher than bread, three times twenty-six. He urges care with good matzos, since Nissan's reishis of mercy shields from Tishrei's judgment.

en: Hashem created the world with the Asarah Maamaros, and through the Ten Makkos He showed openly that every sphere of creation is in His hand.
The makkos refuted both idolatry, with a separate god for each force, and the philosophers' view that Hashem no longer runs the world; He watches over every detail.
Nissan is the reishis of the year, when the world was actually created and Hashem's renewal filters down into nature, and a person should use it to renew himself in avodas Hashem.
Pesach is the time of emunah: Avraham, the first Jew, gave the mitzvah of emunah, and matzah is the food of emunah.
Matzah, three times forty-five, stands higher than bread, three times twenty-six, and a person should take care to have good matzos.

title.en: The Asarah Maamaros revealed in the Ten Makkos

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the three upper and seven lower levels, which grow more tangible as they descend and can be used for good or bad. He explains that through the Ten Makkos Hashem showed that He made the world with the Asarah Maamaros, against those who believe in a separate god for each force, and that the Torah, through the Aseres Hadibros, then contained it all.

title.en: Heavenly and earthly maamaros, makkos in reverse

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Bereishis is the first maamar and the source of the others, followed by three heavenly and then earthly maamaros. The makkos went in reverse order, from the earth up to the heavens, to show against the philosophers that Hashem controls every detail; he notes the sets of seven and three, and mentions that the seder plate and the makkos are also arranged by the ten sefiros.

title.en: Nissan, the reishis and month of renewal

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nissan is the reishis: the world was conceived in Tishrei with judgment but actually created in Nissan with mercy, and the Jewish nation was formed then. Hashem's daily renewal of creation filters down in this month, and he describes how nature awakens in spring after the deadness of winter.

title.en: Renewing oneself in Nissan

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a person should use Nissan to renew himself in avodas Hashem, and tells of a tzaddik who found it hard to take time to answer a question because an hour in Nissan equals a whole day. He asks why a person should lag behind a renewed world, brings the Navi's image of the dry bones rising, and says the new clothes and cleaned house of Pesach should move a person to ask how he himself can become new.

title.en: Avraham, emunah and matzah

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects Nissan as reishis with Avraham Avinu, the first Jew, who gave the first mitzvah, emunah, which the Rambam counts first. Pesach is the time of emunah, and matzah, as the Zohar calls it, is the food of emunah; Avraham, the beginning, also ate matzah.

title.en: Animals, man and the food of man

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each animal was created with one trait, so its behavior can be predicted, while man, to whom every part of creation contributed, holds all ten and each person has his own dominant traits. Bread is therefore the food of man, and he brings the passuk that man lives not by bread alone but by what comes from the mouth of Hashem.

title.en: The Shem Havayah, Shabbos, and matzah above bread

summary.en: The Mashgiach divides the sefiros into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim, as seen in how tefillin straps are wound, and explains the Shem Havayah and its spelled-out form of ten letters. He connects reshus hayachid on Shabbos to Hashem, citing the Zohar, and shows that lechem is three times twenty-six while matzah is three times forty-five, so matzah is far higher.

title.en: Good matzos and the two reishis

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges care to have good, guarded matzos, since on Pesach a person charges himself with emunah for the year. He explains that there are two reishis, Nissan with mercy and Tishrei with judgment, and one who puts himself under Nissan's authority need not fear Rosh Hashanah. He closes with words on renewal.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in Nissan, the Mashgiach explains that at Pesach daas went out of exile and the Jewish people 'became bar mitzvah', and that a boy becomes a baal daas both by reaching the full measure of daas and by accepting the yoke of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach praises the bar mitzvah boy's words on the korban Pesach and brings from the seforim of the Arizal that in Mitzrayim daas was in exile and at Pesach it went free, so the Jews came to daas and became, as it were, bar mitzvah. A boy once asked him why he felt no more daas than the day before; the Mashgiach answers that daas has a fixed measure, like a kezayis or a revi'is, and at thirteen the last drop completes it. This is why the Shabbos before Pesach is Shabbos HaGadol. A second way to become bar mitzvah is like a convert, by accepting the yoke of Heaven, which he ties to 'mishchu u'kchu lachem'. The boy became bar mitzvah on the day of the nasi of Gad, Elyasaf ben De'uel, also called ben Reuel: daas and ratzon together. He closes with the heavenly voice on a bar mitzvah, the gifts one may ask for, and brachos.

en: The Mashgiach brings from the seforim of the Arizal that in Mitzrayim daas was in exile, and at Pesach it went out, so the Jews came to daas.
Daas has a fixed measure like a kezayis or a revi'is; at thirteen the boy has its full measure, even if he cannot feel the last drop.
The Shabbos before Pesach is called Shabbos HaGadol because then the Jewish people became 'gedolim', no longer children.
There is a second way to become bar mitzvah, like a convert: by one's will, accepting the yoke of Heaven.
On the day of a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice tells the boy he is born today and may ask for gifts, and he asks for a heart to understand and to know Hashem.

title.en: Daas goes out of exile; the measure of daas

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the boy's words on the korban Pesach and brings from the Arizal that at Pesach daas left its exile. He answers a bar mitzvah boy who felt no new daas: daas has a fixed measure, like a kezayis or revi'is, completed at thirteen.

title.en: Shabbos HaGadol, the convert, and Elyasaf ben De'uel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Shabbos HaGadol as the day the Jews became gedolim, and shows a second way of becoming bar mitzvah, like a convert who accepts the yoke of Heaven. He ties the boy's day to the nasi of Gad, Elyasaf ben De'uel, also called ben Reuel: daas and ratzon together.

title.en: Gifts from Heaven, the convert's Pesach, and brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the custom of giving a bar mitzvah boy gifts: a heavenly voice tells him he is born today and may ask, and he asks for a heart to understand and to fear Hashem. He brings the Gemara on a convert and the korban Pesach, and closes with brachos for the boy and his family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Succos, the Mashgiach explains why the brachah is made over the lulav, which stands for Yosef the tzaddik, and sees in a bris on Yosef's day of the ushpizin a sign for the child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the four species, which together hold all seven ushpizin: the three hadassim are Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, the two aravos Moshe and Aharon, the lulav Yosef and the esrog Dovid. The Gemara says the brachah is made over the lulav because it is the tallest. He brings the Chasam Sofer's question: the esrog stands for Dovid and malchus, which every brachah mentions, so why not make the brachah over it? The answer is that the lulav is Yosef, the mashpia, who earned the name tzaddik through his test, and he reads 'there is none greater in this house than I' as Yosef defending his rank. Under one custom of the order of ushpizin, this day is Yosef's, and a bris, Yosef's mitzvah of guarding the covenant, on his day is no accident but a good sign for the child. He closes with brachos.

en: The four species correspond to the seven ushpizin: hadassim to the Avos, aravos to Moshe and Aharon, the lulav to Yosef and the esrog to Dovid.
The Chasam Sofer asks why the brachah is not made over the esrog, which stands for Dovid and malchus, the theme of every brachah.
The brachah is made over the lulav because it is Yosef, the mashpia, the one who earned the name tzaddik.
In one order of the ushpizin, this day of Succos belongs to Yosef, and a bris on Yosef's day is by Divine providence, not chance.
The bris is the child's first kedushah and brings him into the level of Yosef the tzaddik, a good sign for his future.

title.en: Why the brachah is over the lulav

summary.en: The Mashgiach matches the four species to the seven ushpizin and brings the Chasam Sofer's question why the brachah is not over the esrog, which stands for Dovid and malchus. He answers that the lulav is Yosef, the mashpia and tzaddik, and reads 'there is none greater in this house than I' in this light.

title.en: A bris on Yosef's day of the ushpizin

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes two orders of the ushpizin, both true; by one custom this day is Yosef's, and a bris meal in the sukkah on Yosef's day, Yosef who excelled in guarding the covenant, is Divine providence and a sign for the child. He closes with brachos for the child and family.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in the days of Sefirah, the Mashgiach explains why the heavenly call 'You are My son' comes in the psalm of 'Why do the nations rage': in a world casting off the yoke of Heaven, the boy must constantly repeat to himself that he is a child of Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'a time for every matter': each boy becomes bar mitzvah in a season suited to him. In these days before Shavuos the Jews purify themselves to stand before Hashem as a 'new offering', newborn, and so too the bar mitzvah boy. He brings from the Zohar that at a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice says 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and Hashem gives new strengths and a yetzer tov; hence the custom of gifts, since He says 'ask of Me and I will give'. He then asks what this has to do with the psalm of 'Why do the nations rage', which Chazal say speaks of the war of Gog and Magog, when the ropes of the yoke of Heaven are torn, as seen in the world today. He answers that once a boy grew up among emunah, but today being a son of Hashem is a great test, so he must, as 'I will tell of the decree' says, keep repeating 'You are My son'. He closes with brachos.

en: Each boy becomes bar mitzvah in a season suited to him; in the days before Shavuos, Jews renew themselves to stand before Hashem as a 'new offering', and so does the bar mitzvah boy.
At a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice proclaims 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and Hashem gives the boy new strengths and a yetzer tov.
The psalm of 'Why do the nations rage' speaks of the time before Moshiach when the yoke of Heaven is cast off, as is seen in the world today.
Once a boy grew up surrounded by emunah; today, exposed to heresy, immodesty and bad middos, being a son of Hashem is a great test.
Therefore, as 'I will tell of the decree' teaches, the boy must constantly repeat to himself that he is a child of Hashem and keep his bar mitzvah day fresh.

title.en: A new offering: the bar mitzvah as a rebirth

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the bar mitzvah to its season: before Shavuos, Jews renew themselves as a 'new offering' to Hashem, and so does the boy. He brings from the Zohar that a heavenly voice calls 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and explains the custom of bar mitzvah gifts by 'ask of Me and I will give'.

title.en: 'You are My son' in the psalm of Gog and Magog

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the bar mitzvah has to do with the psalm 'Why do the nations rage', which Chazal apply to the war of Gog and Magog, when the yoke of Heaven is torn off, as he sees in the world today. He contrasts earlier generations, when a boy grew up surrounded by emunah, with today, when being a son of Hashem is a great test.

title.en: 'I will tell of the decree': repeating 'You are My son'

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'I will tell of the decree' as a law to repeat constantly that one is a child of Hashem and not act like those who go other ways. He tells the boy to keep his bar mitzvah day and its resolutions fresh, brings that the day should be celebrated like a wedding, and closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 3, the Mashgiach explains how Chochmah and Binah give birth to love and fear of Hashem, and how Da'as, deep and lasting concentration, makes those middos genuine and lasting.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the weeks of Sefirah, when the middos are refined, since good middos are the prerequisite for Torah. He then reads Tanya chapter 3: the soul has intellect (Chochmah, Binah, Da'as) and middos, and the intellect is the father and mother of the middos, with Da'as as the bridge that controls them; a bowl of cookies and a gifted child who is not yet responsible illustrate this. Chochmah is the flash of insight, Binah builds it up like bricks. Contemplating Hashem's greatness first produces yirah, a sense of shame before His greatness, and only afterwards true ahavah, the soul's thirst to cling to Hashem. A digression on Shechem and Dina explains the fiery words of love. Finally, Da'as means intense and lengthy concentration; without it love and fear are only empty imaginings. He ends with refining the middos through Sefirah.

en: Chochmah and Binah are the father and mother of the middos, and Da'as is the bridge that unites intellect with emotion and controls it.
Chochmah is a sudden flash of new insight whose origin a person does not know; Binah builds on it thought by thought until a complete structure stands.
Although ahavah ranks higher than yirah, in attaining them yirah must come first; genuine ahavah follows as a gift from Hashem.
True yirah is not fear of punishment but shame before Hashem's greatness, that so small a creature should go against His will.
Ahavah is the soul's yearning to cling to Hashem, like the fire in the heart that thirsts for the water of Chochmah.
Da'as is strong and lengthy concentration on Hashem's greatness; without it, love and fear are only imaginings.

title.en: Sefirah, middos and the text of chapter 3

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that middos are refined during Sefirah because they are the prerequisite for Torah, and links each chapter of Pirkei Avos to that week's middah. He then reads Tanya chapter 3: the soul is divided into intellect, Chochmah, Binah and Da'as, and middos, which are born of the intellect.

title.en: Da'as as the bridge: cookies and a katan

summary.en: Chochmah and Binah give birth to the middos, and Da'as is the bridge that unites them. With a jar of cookies the Mashgiach shows how understanding produces desire and how Da'as, responsibility, holds it in check; a child may be a genius but is not yet a bar da'as.

title.en: Chochmah as a flash, Binah as building

summary.en: Applied to avodas Hashem, seeing and contemplating Hashem's greatness gives birth to love or fear. The Mashgiach defines the intellect as the power in the mind that produces thought: Chochmah, koach mah, is a sudden flash of insight from Hashem, and Binah, from binyan, builds it brick by brick into a complete understanding.

title.en: Birchas Yotzer: fear, then love

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the birth of the middos in davening: in Birchas Yotzer one contemplates the greatness of creation and produces yirah, then in Ahavah Rabbah the great love of Hashem for Klal Yisroel arouses love in return, leading to the self-sacrifice of Krias Shema. This requires thinking deeply, not running through the words.

title.en: Why yirah must come before ahavah

summary.en: Though ahavah is the higher middah, genuine love can only come after fear. Fear is within a person's choice, love is not, as the spinach example shows; once a person has yirah, Hashem grants ahavah, the 'avodas matanah'. The Mashgiach brings the Maggid's words on the way of the 'ish' and a Gemara that yirah first is a good sign.

title.en: Higher fear is shame before greatness

summary.en: The Tanya begins with the higher fear of Hashem's greatness, not the lower fear of punishment. The Mashgiach compares it to everyone rising when a president enters, and brings the Gemara that yirah is busha, shame, and the reading of Bereishis as 'yarei boshes'. After the fear the heart flames with love.

title.en: The words of love by Shechem and Dina

summary.en: The four expressions of love in the Tanya appear in the parsha of Shechem and Dina. The Mashgiach explains that Shechem carried sparks of kedushah: he and Dina were reincarnated as Zimri and Kozbi and later as Rabbi Akiva and his wife, and their daughter became Osnas, Yosef's wife. The fierce words of love reflect those sparks struggling to break free of the klipah.

title.en: Love as the soul's thirst

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach says every Jew who unites his Chochmah and Binah can come to a burning love for Hashem, klos hanefesh, like a thirsty man in the desert who sees water. The fire in the heart thirsts for the water of Chochmah, the point of G-dliness in the soul; the other middos are branches of love and fear.

title.en: Da'as: intense and lasting focus

summary.en: Da'as, from 'yada', means connecting: to give birth one must fix the mind with strength and for a long time on Hashem's greatness, or the love and fear will be only empty imaginings. Da'as sustains the middos. The Mashgiach closes on purifying the middos during Sefirah, comparing the last weeks to refining silver to sterling.
